title: 7 cap table mistakes (and how to avoid them)
summary: Messy spreadsheets = costly cap table errors. Protect ownership & investor trust with a clean, accurate single source of truth.
body_markdown:
For many founders and CFOs, cap tables start as a quick spreadsheet—“good enough” until the stakes rise. But that false sense of security is dangerous. Misallocated shares, missing option grants, and unclear ownership don’t just create confusion; they demotivate employees and spook investors. Left unchecked, these errors can spiral into costly, time-consuming legal battles.


Fixing cap table mistakes often requires legal fees and updated filings. Reconciling with employees or investors can make the process more expensive than catching errors early. A messy or inaccurate cap table can derail fundraising, erode investor confidence, and quietly chip away at founder ownership and control.


Startups may miss cap table mistakes until an investor or early employee uncovers them. By then, it's often too late. Let's review the basics, and then go over 7 common cap table mistakes that can cost you down the line.


## What is a cap table, and why does it matter?


A cap table, or capitalization table, is a record of who owns what in your company. It tracks founders, employees, and investors, showing exactly who controls the company and how ownership is allocated. Think of it as the single source of truth for[your company’s equity](https://pulley.com/guides/the-startup-founders-guide-to-equity) .


Cap tables include several key components:


- **Founder equity:** This is the starting point for most cap tables. It shows how much of the company each founder owns, and how you structure your control and decision-making authority. Keeping this clear helps avoid misunderstandings down the road.
- **Investor shares:** As your startup raises money in[angel, seed, or venture rounds](https://support.crunchbase.com/hc/en-us/articles/115010458467-Glossary-of-Funding-Types) , you issue shares to investors. The cap table records who invested, how much, and what percentage of your company they own, giving you a snapshot of who has a financial stake in your success.
- **Employee equity:** Many companies create an equity pool for employees, usually in the form of stock options. This helps attract and retain top talent, and also aligns employees’ incentives with the company’s long-term growth.
- **Convertible instruments:** Tools like[SAFEs (simple agreements for future equity)](https://pulley.com/guides/what-is-a-simple-agreement-for-future-equity-safe) and[convertible notes](https://www.investopedia.com/terms/c/convertibles.asp) start as promises of future ownership. They eventually convert into equity, often at the next funding round. Tracking them on the cap table won’t stop dilution, but it ensures you and your investors aren’t caught off guard by how ownership changes.
- **Share classes:** Not all shares are created equal. Some share classes may carry special voting rights, preferred dividends, or liquidation preferences. Documenting these details ensures you know who has influence over big decisions and how to distribute returns if you sell the company.


Using a[cap table template](https://pulley.com/templates/cap-table-template) alongside a[409A valuation](https://pulley.com/guides/what-is-a-409a-valuation) can help founders stay organized and ensure they accurately price equity for investors and employees.


### Why investors and founders care about cap tables


Investors and founders care about cap tables because ownership drives incentives and trust. A clear cap table signals your readiness for audits, builds confidence with investors, and helps motivate employees.


A messy cap table hinders fundraising, causes disputes, and hurts morale. Keeping your cap table clean and accurate helps everyone make better decisions. It also helps founders maintain control, align employees through equity, and avoid unexpected dilution.


## 7 cap table mistakes (and how to avoid them)


Cap tables can make or break a startup’s success, yet many teams ignore them early on. Learning the most common mistakes and how to avoid them helps keep equity ownership clear and investors confident.


### 1. Not creating a cap table early


Many founders wait to document equity until investors ask for it, but this delay can create disputes and confusion about who owns what. Creating a cap table on day one, even if your company is just an idea, sets expectations and prevents surprises. Pulley makes it easy to start a cap table immediately, so you can track ownership accurately from the first grant. Consider starting a cap table even before incorporation, so that when you do incorporate, you're ready to build your provisional cap table in to a formal legal cap table.


### 2. Not keeping your cap table clean and updated


Outdated cap tables create hidden risks. Missing grants, unissued shares, or mistakes can frustrate investors and slow down fundraising. Employees can also lose trust if they feel they don’t own what was promised. Updating your cap table with every equity event keeps your numbers transparent and fundraising on track. Compliance risks introduced by neglecting your cap table early on could haunt you well in to your company's future.


### 3. Using spreadsheets instead of cap table software


Excel sheets work well early on, but they break under complexity.[SAFEs](https://pulley.com/guides/what-is-a-simple-agreement-for-future-equity-safe) , convertible notes, pro-rata rights, and future dilution are hard to model correctly, and broken formulas are common.


Switching to real-time cap table software lets you track everything automatically and model future rounds accurately. Pulley provides a live cap table that updates instantly with each equity change, reducing errors and saving time. Additionally many investors may *require* the use of a cap table provider.


### 4. Founder dilution and dead equity


Over-dilution raises red flags for future investors. To maintain control, you should regularly track founder ownership percentages, remove inactive stakeholders, implement vesting schedules, and clean up dead equity. Regularly reviewing your cap table helps you[model dilution](https://pulley.com/guides/what-is-a-simple-agreement-for-future-equity-safe) and plan future funding rounds. Simple recurring tasks like canceling unvested equity from departed employees and returning it to the option pool, if not completed and tracked correctly, can create ownership misunderstandings and distort cap table percentages later.


### 5. Ignoring the impacts of convertible instruments and option pools


Unmodeled SAFEs, convertible notes, or[option pools](https://pulley.com/guides/option-pool) can create sudden dilution at the worst possible moment. Founders may only notice the impact when a priced round closes.


Modeling these instruments early gives you a clear picture of future ownership and helps you plan both option pool size and financing strategies. Pulley’s built-in dilution[modeling tool](https://pulley.com/products/fundraising/fundraising-modeling) lets you simulate the effect of SAFEs and option pools, so you can make informed decisions before rounds close.


### 6. Over-engineering your cap table


Adding too many share classes, special terms, or unusual clauses can create unnecessary complexity and raises questions from investors. Keeping your cap table simple and focused reduces confusion and ensures the right incentives are in place without overcomplicating ownership.


### 7. Not optimizing for people


If you don’t structure equity to acquire top talent and motivate your team, it can lower morale. Employees may not fully understand their equity ownership, which can make recruiting and retention harder. Optimizing for your people means clearly communicating equity and aligning incentives so everyone sees how their role drives the company’s success.


## Take control of your cap table before it controls you


A clean, well-maintained cap table is your record of ownership. It helps you keep everything clear, aligned, and ready for growth. Taking the right approach helps you plan financing strategically and makes sure equity works as intended for everyone involved.

## FAQs about common cap table mistakes


### What's the most common cap table mistake founders make?


The biggest mistake is waiting too long to audit and fix your cap table. Founders often ignore issues until later, but by then, confusion, disputes, and investor mistrust have crept in.


### How early should you create your cap table?


You should create your cap table on day one. Even if it feels too early, documenting ownership right away prevents misunderstandings and gives you a solid foundation as you start growing.


### What happens when your cap table isn't updated regularly?


An outdated cap table erodes trust with investors and employees. Pulley automatically updates after every grant or financing, so you always have a real-time record that is audit- and investor-ready.


### Can spreadsheets keep up as your startup grows?

### How much founder equity should you protect?


There is no single magic number, but you should always keep enough to stay motivated and credible with investors. Protecting meaningful ownership ensures long-term control and healthy decision-making.


### Do unmodeled SAFEs or option pools create surprises?

### How do I know if my cap table is investor-ready?
